question: What is the main job of the endocrine system in the human body?

options.C: Regulating body processes using chemical messengers

explanation: The endocrine system uses hormones released into the bloodstream to coordinate slow, steady body activities across different organs. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h1)

question: How does endocrine signaling differ from nervous system signaling?

options.A: Nervous system responses last much longer than endocrine responses
options.B: Nervous signals target only the pancreas and adrenals
options.C: Endocrine communication needs direct cell-to-cell contact
options.D: Endocrine signals rely on hormones travelling through blood to produce slower effects

explanation: Hormones travel through the blood to reach distant cells, taking more time to work but lasting longer than fast nerve impulses. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h1)

question: Where are the receptors for steroid hormones usually found inside a cell?

options.C: Attached to the outer blood vessel walls
options.D: Embedded on the outer cell membrane

explanation: Steroid hormones easily pass through cell membranes, so their receptors are located inside the cell rather than on the surface. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h2)

question: Which type of hormone is made of amino acid chains and dissolves easily in blood?
explanation: Peptide hormones are water-soluble proteins that travel freely in the bloodstream without needing carrier proteins. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h2)

question: What is the name of the large inactive protein formed first during peptide hormone creation?
explanation: Ribosomes first build a preprohormone, which is then processed inside the cell to become an active hormone. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h3)

question: Why must peptide hormones be cut by enzymes inside the Golgi apparatus?

options.A: To attach carrier proteins so it can dissolve
options.B: To turn larger starter proteins into smaller active hormones
options.C: To destroy the hormone before it enters the blood
options.D: To turn cholesterol into amino acid chains

explanation: Enzymes trim the larger protein inside the cell to create the final active hormone before it is released. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h3)

question: What is the essential foundational precursor molecule used to manufacture all steroid hormones?
explanation: All steroid hormones share a sterol ring structure derived directly from cholesterol molecules. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h4)

question: Why are steroid hormones not stored in large amounts inside cell vesicles?

options.A: They pass freely through cell membranes
options.C: They break down instantly in cell fluid
options.D: They are too large to fit in standard vesicles

explanation: Because steroid hormones easily cross cell membranes, they cannot be contained in storage sacs and must be made as needed. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h4)

question: Through which process do peptide hormone vesicles release their contents into the blood?
explanation: Storage sacs merge with the outer cell membrane, pushing their hormone contents outside the cell through exocytosis. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h5)

question: How do steroid-producing cells respond when told to release more hormone?

options.A: They convert stored proteins into active peptides
options.B: They open large membrane gates to empty stored sacs
options.C: They pull circulating hormones back from the blood
options.D: They quickly make new hormones from cholesterol on demand

explanation: Since they do not store ready-made hormones, steroid-producing glands must manufacture them immediately when stimulated. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h5)

question: What type of feedback loop does the body use most often to keep hormone levels balanced?
explanation: Negative feedback works to reverse changes in hormone levels, stopping further release once the normal balance is restored. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h6)

question: What happens when hormone levels in the blood get too high in a negative feedback system?

options.A: It forces storage sacs to release all remaining reserves
options.B: It slows down the release of upstream stimulating hormones
options.C: It makes the gland switch to producing different hormones

explanation: High hormone levels signal the brain and pituitary gland to reduce further hormone production. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h6)

question: Which two major organs are mainly responsible for clearing hormones from the body?
explanation: The liver breaks down hormones, and the kidneys filter the waste products out through the urine. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h7)

question: Why do steroid hormones usually stay active in the blood longer than peptide hormones?

options.A: They cannot be broken down by the liver
options.B: They are stored inside kidney tissues
options.C: They bind to carrier proteins that protect them from quick breakdown
options.D: They change their amino acid sequence to resist breakdown

explanation: Proteins in the blood attach to steroid hormones, shielding them from rapid destruction by the liver. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h7)

question: What term describes a medical condition caused by too much hormone production?
explanation: Hypersecretion means the body is producing too much of a hormone, often due to an overactive gland or small tumor. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h8)

question: A patient has fatigue, weight gain, and cold intolerance because of a sluggish thyroid gland. How is this classified?
explanation: When a gland produces too little hormone, the condition is known as hyposecretion. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h8)
